claim: Certainty effect: people overvalue sure outcomes relative to merely probable ones, reversing preferences when both probabilities are scaled down (Problems 1/2 and 3/4/7/8 of the 1979 paper: 82% vs 83% at N=72; 80% vs 65% at N=95; 86% vs 73% at N=66).
schema_part: G (do not assume EV-driven choice when a sure option exists); background
agent_test: Give the agent matched sure-vs-probable item pairs at equal tokens; count reversals vs a scaffold-free run.

claim: Reflection effect: risk-averse for gains, risk-seeking for losses (Problem 3: 80% sure gain; Problem 3 prime: 92% gamble over sure loss, N=95).
agent_test: Mirror gain/loss item pairs; measure whether the agent's risk attitude flips only with wording.

claim: Isolation effect: shared components are ignored, so identical final prospects get different choices when staged differently (Problem 10: 78% of 141 chose the sure branch although Problem 4 gave 35% for the same final prospect).
agent_test: Pose staged vs collapsed versions of the same prospects; test whether a final-state rewrite step removes the gap.

claim: Very small probabilities are overweighted: lottery tickets and insurance both attractive (Problem 14: 72% took 1-in-1000 for 5,000; Problem 14 prime: 83% chose a sure loss of 5; N=72 each).
agent_test: Rare-event items with description format; compare agent weighting to human inverse-S.

claim: The 1979 patterns replicate in a preregistered multinational test: 94% of items, 12 of 13 contrasts, N=4,098, 19 countries, 13 languages, with attenuated effects and heterogeneity across countries.
agent_test: Use these items as the LLM test battery; the replication confirms they are valid probes. (a10 and b04 are the same paper.)

claim: Mean loss aversion across the human literature is about 1.95 (Bayesian CrI 1.82-2.11; 607 estimates, 150 articles), below the oft-cited 2.25, which was the median of 25 unincentivised graduate students.
agent_test: Use 1.7-2.0 as the human reference, not 2.25, when scoring agent loss aversion.
audit: downgraded 2026-11-20 by check_established.py: only 1 opened source(s) from distinct authors

claim: There is modest publication bias in loss aversion: bias-corrected mean 1.742 [1.674, 1.811]; working papers about 0.25 lower (about 1.73); study covariates explain only 15.5% of variance.
agent_test: None direct; set the benchmark target to 1.7-1.9.

claim: Reported loss-aversion estimates are heavily skewed: aggregate-level mean 1.95 (median 1.52, n=281); individual-level means 2.94 (median 1.80, n=160); overall range 0.04 to 23.46. Medians are safer than means.
agent_test: Report medians and intervals when scoring the agent.

claim: Loss aversion depends on the range of gains and losses in the task: it vanishes (about 1.0) or reverses (0.8-0.9) when losses have the wider range, and is 1.6-2.3 when gains have the wider range (Walasek and Stewart 2015, four experiments, N=88-429; Rakow et al. 2020 replicate).
agent_test: Run the same mixed-gamble set with gain-wide vs loss-wide ranges; check if lambda follows range as in people.

claim: Loss aversion is contested as a universal preference: critics attribute effects to status quo, attention, inertia, small-stakes absence and endowment alternatives. Only review-level evidence was read; Gal and Rucker and Yechiam were seen in snippets.
agent_test: None; treat lambda as context-dependent, not a trait.

claim: Accountability does not reduce loss aversion: Vieider's finding failed to replicate in two new experiments and a close direct replication with almost twice the sample (Bayesian: substantial evidence for no difference).
agent_test: None.

claim: Decisions from experience reverse the rare-event pattern: rare events are underweighted when learned by sampling (description-experience gap). A meta-analysis exists but its numbers were not read.
schema_part: O (for agents given simulated histories vs descriptions)
agent_test: Present the same prospects as descriptions and as sampled histories (20 and 100 draws); measure the gap.
audit: downgraded 2026-11-20 by check_established.py: only 1 opened source(s) from distinct authors

claim: Competing explanation: the fourfold pattern also appears in a no-risk mirror condition (Oprea 2024), suggesting it can come from complexity-driven heuristics, not probability weighting; a reply (Banki et al. 2025) says participants were confused. No LLM test of the mirror pattern was found (gap search); Hintze et al. 2025 report LLM weighting resembles decisions from experience, not the inverse S.
agent_test: Add a no-risk mirror control to LLM tests; if the pattern persists, it is not about probability weighting.

claim: Prospect-theory patterns extend beyond money, e.g. travel prizes in 1979 and information with no money value (loss framing, endowment, Asian-disease with facts).
agent_test: Test the agent on non-monetary loss framing.

claim: LLMs show some prospect-theory biases but not all: GPT-3 showed 3 of 6 K&T 1979 biases (framing, certainty effect, overweighting of 1% vs 2%); only the largest GPT-3 model beat chance on choices13k (t(29134) = -16.85).
agent_test: Re-run the six K&T biases on current models (only GPT-3 was tested).

claim: LLM loss aversion is weaker than human on average: pooled lambda 1.26 [1.06, 1.46] across 11 studies, 32 models, 102 estimates (prediction interval 0.20-2.31); matches humans in symmetric designs (1.15 vs 1.07) but far below in losses-smaller-than-gains designs (1.46 vs about 2.3).
agent_test: Fit lambda to the agent with a symmetric and an asymmetric design; compare to the pooled numbers.

claim: Model-level fitted prospect-theory parameters are unstable and method-dependent: curvature is 1.01 under the TK fit and 0.52 under Tanaka; small LLMs (Llama-3.1-8B, Qwen2.5-14B) fail fit criteria; verbal probability markers shift parameters, especially lambda.
schema_part: G (prefer numeric probabilities to verbal ones in the schema)
agent_test: Compare parameters under numeric vs verbal probabilities at equal tokens.

claim: Prompt-dependence of LLM loss aversion: telling a model that humans are loss averse makes it so (ChatGPT lambda 1.09 baseline, 1.785 after the Brown abstract, 1.043 after a paper reporting none); persona and role-play also move it.
schema_part: G (guard against priming by task framing)
agent_test: Prime the agent with biased vs unbiased literature and see if choices move; add a neutral-prior guard.

claim: Prompting instructions to be risk/loss averse barely move GPT-4; examples work, two examples confound; zero-shot chain of thought does not move it toward rationality. All from one paper.
agent_test: Compare label vs one-example prompts at equal tokens.

claim: Reasoning models act near expected-value maximisers (correlation 0.86-1 with risk-neutral); conversational models less so (below 0.5) and sensitive to framing, order and explanation; all show a description-history gap.
agent_test: At equal tokens, compare a deliberation-first agent vs a direct-answer agent on framing-flip items.

claim: LLMs predict and simulate human gambles as more rational than people: GPT-4o Spearman 0.94 with max-EV when predicting vs humans 0.48 (choices13k). Zero-shot, as themselves, GPT-4-Turbo and GPT-4o reach only 0.41 and 0.28 (a different question).
agent_test: Do not use the agent as a simulator of human risky choice without calibration.

claim: Framing effects in LLMs are scenario-dependent: ChatGPT rated a drug 5 vs 4 in every trial (humans 5.2 vs 4.6, t(80)=3.86); Payne 2025 saw 85.6% vs 0.8% flips in one scenario, a reversal in another, and none in pure symbols (100% indifference); 57-85% contradictory answers across framings in three models.
schema_part: G (re-express problem neutrally and check consistency)
agent_test: Ask each item in gain and loss wording; compare consistency with vs without a neutralise-wording step.

claim: Instruction tuning and RLHF increase the certainty effect: pretrained bases score 0.00 (DaVinci), 0.09 (T5), 0.03 (Mistral); tuned versions 0.24 (DaVinci-002), 0.67 (DaVinci-003), 0.17 (Flan-T5), 0.29 (Mistral-Instruct). Product-choice templates, 2023 models; no lambda contrast exists.
agent_test: Compare base vs tuned variants if available.

claim: GPT budget choices are more internally consistent (CCEI 0.997-0.999, GARP-violation-free in 81-95 of 100) than human choices (0.963-0.985) but break under language reframing.
agent_test: Use revealed-preference consistency as a cheap check of the agent.

claim: Awareness prompting reduces biased framing and status-quo prompts in admission decisions (to 17.2% and 8.5% as read from two-column text; uncertain).
agent_test: Re-read the numbers. Test awareness prompt vs none.

claim: Original 1992 CPT parameters (alpha=beta=0.88, lambda=2.25, 25 graduate students) are confirmed via Brown et al.; the weighting benchmark 0.65 used by Tarabeih (2026) equals the mean of gamma 0.61 and delta 0.69, which fits the remembered values, but the 1992 primary text was still not obtained.
agent_test: Use the Tanaka 2010 benchmark (0.670/2.630/0.685) as Wang et al. do when fitting agents.

claim: Current reasoning models are close to expected-value maximisers on plain numeric gambles and weakly loss averse: 2025-26 models take the higher-EV gamble on 94.3-99.9% of trials (gpt-5-nano, gpt-5.2, grok-4.3, gemini-3-flash, kimi-k2.5), lambda 1.005-1.28 in focal models; reasoning models correlate 0.86-1.0 with an EV agent.
schema_part: G/S (an EV check step is cheap on numeric items)
agent_test: Run verbatim 1979 problems (1, 2, 3, 3', 4, 7, 8, 10) on current reasoning models; this specific test is still missing (gap 1).

claim: The same reasoning models still flip with narrative framing when the problem is a story: o3 and Claude Sonnet 4 with thinking show framing effects of +1.40 to +1.84 (championship, 85.6% vs 0.8% BLITZ), a reverse effect in career transition (-0.37 to -0.60) and near zero in business merger; effect size is not tied to how often the model calculated EV.
agent_test: Re-run Payne's scenarios with and without a neutralise-wording step at equal tokens.

claim: Stripping a story to symbolic final-outcome maths removes the frame effect: o3 declared indifference in 200/200 and GPT-4o in 196/200 equal-EV maths items; when forced to choose, both always picked the sure option.
agent_test: Compare story vs maths-form vs chain-of-thought-only at equal tokens (gap 2 still open: no head-to-head vs plain CoT).

claim: A description-history gap exists in all 20 tested LLMs: modest for frontier reasoning models (GPT-5.1, DeepSeek-R1 correlation with EV agent stays about 0.98), large for conversational and small open reasoning models; 100 draws do not remove it and context length is not the cause.
schema_part: G (do not let the agent learn risk from a few simulated draws)
agent_test: Give an agent 20 vs 100 simulated draws and compare with the stated-probability version.

claim: Reports of loss aversion in the agent's context shift its lambda toward the reported level even when sample size is tiny (n=43 vs 10,583: interaction p=.75), and a joint-evaluation prompt (judge all lotteries together) reduces the shift except when gains equal losses.
agent_test: Test delayed priming inside a multi-step agent that reads papers, with and without the joint-evaluation guard (gap 4 still open for delayed priming).

claim: LLM agents show reference-point-dependent loss-averse behaviour in trading settings, in direction but model-dependent: GPT-4o sells 97 of 100 in G+ and 85 in G- (price off its peak); Qwen-2.5-7B keeps realising gains regardless; prompted strong-loss-aversion agents switch style less (rank-biserial 0.47-0.67, 4 models).
schema_part: G (state the reference point explicitly in multi-step tasks)
agent_test: Vary the stated reference point (purchase price vs peak vs expectation) in a multi-step task and measure choice shifts (gap 7 partly closed).

claim: Fixed-model lambda is repeatable at temperature up to 0.7 (coefficient of variation < 0.15) and noisy at T=1.0 (> 0.30); probability weighting is not repeatable (intra-class correlation 0.62); between-model lambda spans 0.01 to 4.0 in one study.
schema_part: G (do not trust one-shot parameter estimates)
agent_test: Repeat a lambda elicitation 10 times at T=0, 0.7, 1.0 for the agent's model (gap 9 only partly closed: the repeat-stability evidence is one preprint appendix).

claim: No published test of the Oprea no-risk mirror pattern in LLMs was found; LLM probability weighting is inconsistent with the human inverse S in early studies (GPT-4 resembles decisions from experience), so the complexity-heuristic reading is untested.
agent_test: Add a deterministic disaggregated-payment control to an LLM weighting test.

claim: Human loss aversion is design- and stake-dependent: reviews argue that small losses are often not overweighted and that evidence does not show losses loom larger on balance; the description-experience gap is robust but depends on problem structure and persists when sampling error is removed.
schema_part: G (do not assume lambda about 2 as the human default)
agent_test: Compare LLM lambda against design-matched human values, as Tarabeih does.

claim: The certainty effect in people shrinks when probabilities are shown as identifiable events: preference shift for the safe option -39 points with percentages vs -12 with a 00-99 draw (diff-in-diff z=2.34, p=.019).
agent_test: Test whether the same concrete re-expression shrinks LLM sure-vs-probable reversals.

claim: LLM feelings ratings invert the loss-aversion asymmetry: gains rated stronger than equivalent losses in 8 of 9 post-trained models (scale difference +1.2 to +24.3), linearising to 0.98-0.99 when outcomes are rated jointly; choices show no such asymmetry (lambda 0.88-1.59).
agent_test: Not an agent-schema item; background.
